entities.name: Abbadid dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Abbadid dynasty (c. 1023-1091 CE) was a Muslim Arab dynasty that ruled Seville (Ishbiliyya) as an independent taifa kingdom during al-Andalus's fragmentation period following the collapse of the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba. Despite ruling for less than 70 years, the Abbadids created one of the most brilliant cultural courts of the taifa period, with the last Abbadid ruler al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad (r. 1069-1091) being the most celebrated Arabic poet-king of medieval Iberia.

The taifa period (1031-1085 CE) followed the Umayyad Caliphate's collapse, fragmenting al-Andalus into small competing kingdoms. The Abbadids rose under Abu al-Qasim Muhammad, a Seville judge who exploited the chaos to establish independence. Under his son al-Mu'tadid (r. 1042-1069) and grandson al-Mu'tamid, Seville expanded to control most of southern Iberia.

Al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad is remembered as one of the greatest Arabic poets and a tragic figure: a cultivated ruler who wrote exquisite poetry about love, wine, and nature while presiding over political collapse. When Alfonso VI of Castile captured Toledo in 1085 threatening all of Iberia, al-Mu'tamid invited the Almoravids from North Africa, who expelled Alfonso but then took al-Mu'tamid prisoner in 1091, ending the Abbadid dynasty. Al-Mu'tamid died in exile in Morocco in 1095, writing his most moving poems in captivity.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Abbadid dynasty's cultural brilliance and its tragic end — al-Mu'tamid dying in exile writing poetry — embody the Andalusian taifa era's paradox of cultural splendor amid political collapse, making it the most poignant chapter in al-Andalus's history.
